item.itunes:author: 獨角獸那麼叫
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUqJ2OBfB6s

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開台灣國產鮮乳與進口鮮乳保存期限巨大差異背後的真正原因。
  • 釐清大眾及主流媒體長年誤將台灣鮮乳視為「低溫殺菌」的認知盲區與事實真相。
  • 深入分析業界代表在訪談中「只說一半實話」如何無形中誤導消費者對風味與品質的判斷。

摘要

百靈果專訪鮮乳坊引發的保存期爭議

作者指出，知名Podcast節目《百靈果》在專訪鮮乳坊創辦人時，主持人凱莉提出了一個民眾普遍好奇的核心疑問：為何台灣鮮乳的保存期限通常只有約十三天，而進口鮮乳卻能保存三十天甚至八、九十天？面對該提問，受訪者僅表示國外也有短效期的鮮乳、不同殺菌方式會影響保存期限與口感，並提及梅納反應對風味的影響，卻始終未正面解釋關鍵的差異本質，令許多期待聽到真相的觀眾感到受訪者在刻意迴避。

台灣鮮乳普遍採用超高溫殺菌的真相

作者進一步強調，一般民眾容易誤以為台灣鮮乳之所以保存期限短，是因為採用了歐美常見的72度低溫巴氏殺菌；但事實上，農業數據與消基會資料均證實，台灣高達99%的鮮乳都是採用125度至138度的超高溫滅菌（UHT）技術。國產鮮乳與進口乳在殺菌溫度上並無顯著較低，甚至殺菌溫度可能更高，然而台灣鮮乳卻只能冷藏保存不到兩週。作者質疑，這其中的關鍵其實是無菌充填技術與保存條件，受訪者卻將問題歸咎於殺菌溫度差異，完全偏離了核心事實。

只說一半的實話對消費者認知的誤導

作者認為，在訪談中「只說一半的實話」比說錯話更為嚴重，因為缺少關鍵資訊會導致觀眾自行腦補錯誤結論，甚至連主流媒體記者都長年誤報台灣鮮乳是低溫殺菌。此外，受訪者稱進口乳因高溫產生梅納反應而風味不如鮮乳純淨，但事實上台灣各大品牌同樣採用超高溫殺菌，若依此邏輯也會產生梅納反應。作者呼籲乳品產業應公開透明地呈現完整科學事實，而非利用資訊落差與避重就輕的話術誤導消費者對國產鮮乳與進口乳的認知。

================================================

The Bailingguo podcast invited the founder of Milk Man; this interview is incredibly packed with insights. For instance, Kylie asked, "Why does Taiwanese fresh milk expire so quickly? ""Foreign milk can last for 30 days." Anyone who knows the truth about Taiwan’s fresh milk must think that was a great question, right? So satisfying! Asking him directly to his face to see how he’d answer—yeah, why is that? The comments section also felt it hit the nail on the head, but naturally, he didn't really answer it; he just dodged the question. For those of you who know the truth, let's not spoil it yet. For viewers watching on a computer, I suggest opening the original interview video as well and checking each segment along the timeline; if the original. makes you want to roll your eyes, you can come back here to see how he actually responded. He said that abroad there is also shorter-shelf-life milk, that everyone uses different sterilization methods, and with Taiwan's current methods, it's about two weeks and must be refrigerated; there’s a difference in flavor and texture, and some people don't like the Maillard reaction taste, so [his] fresh milk is purer. It looks like he answered it, right? Different shelf lives because domestic and foreign sterilization methods differ, but that’s not what the audience wants to know. "Everyone uses different sterilization methods"—who is "everyone"? When you say "different," who exactly is being compared to whom? You replied that there is also short-shelf-life milk abroad, usually at 72 to 75 degrees for 15 seconds, sold locally for quick consumption; that statement itself isn't wrong, but what Kylie was asking about was the imported milk we see in Taiwan—why is its shelf life longer? Now, can I be the one to ask? Hitting the nail on the head isn't enough; we need to cut to the bone and ask who is being compared to whom: when Taiwan's Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Richi, Lin Fengying, or even your Milk Man, are compared to American imports like Costco’s Kirkland or Foremost, why can theirs last 85 or 90 days while. Taiwan's only lasts 13? "Different sterilization methods"—how, exactly, are they different? When viewers see that Taiwan's fresh milk only lasts 13 days, might they think it's the same 72- degree low-temperature pasteurization used locally in Europe and America? How innocent, how kind—so it's different from the ultra-high temperature used for imported milk? The truth is, Taiwan's fresh milk is all ultra-high temperature ! Isn't the agricultural data right here ? 99%is UHT; the Consumers 'Foundation also says Taiwanese milk is basically long-life milk, 125 to 135 degrees, while imported milk is 135 or 138 degrees—how many degrees lower is that,. really? So is*this*what you meant by " different"? Let's look at the dairy industry: 138 degrees for 1.5 to 2 seconds, yet it only lasts 13 days refrigerated. Australian UHT milk is 135 degrees for 1 to 2 seconds and can be stored at room temperature for 12 months . Yes, the sterilization methods are different. Domestic milk is three degrees higher than imported milk. It's different, but because it's at a higher temperature, the shelf life is actually shorter? Is that how it works? Or is it because there's no aseptic filling? Although some comments felt it was spot on, others felt the guest was shifting the focus and dodging questions, only saying what they wanted to say. Look,. they addressed the previous sentence about fresh milk quite directly, then immediately switched to other topics, starting to talk about raw milk consumption in the US fitness community . So, what about the sterilization temperature and shelf life that everyone wanted to know about? Dodged. They didn't answer. That's why the audience feels like vomiting blood watching this . I'm not taking things out of context. Seriously, the timeline is down below; you can all go back and check the original video. The female host's complete question should have been, " Taiwan uses such high temperatures of over 130 degrees for sterilization, so why can it still only last 13 days?" Your dairy products are at 138 degrees, plus or minus two. This temperature is.

even higher than many in Europe and America, so why is it still only 13 days ? If you only intended for it to last 13 days anyway, why use such a high temperature? Pasteurization at 72 degrees lasts 13 days, and sterilization at 138 degrees still only lasts 13 days , so wasn't that high heat for nothing? If you asked that on the spot, let's see how they could dodge it! Exactly, why didn't they press them for an answer? Everyone wanted to hear it. Right, if the local sentiment in Taiwan is really like that, and so many people truly don't know that Taiwan's fresh milk uses ultra-high heat, mistakenly believing it's low-temperature and pure, no wonder the industry is desperate to amend the law to monopolize the term "fresh milk" for domestic use only. So why does the audience feel like vomiting blood? At that moment, you just want to smash the screen and jump in to ask yourself. There was even a comment telling me to come and take a class. I guess the implication is that I don't understand milk, I just don't know how to say Taiwan's fresh milk is the best in the world. Let me take a step back and explain where the problem with this interview lies. It's not that what the industry representatives said was wrong ; much of the knowledge is professional when taken in isolation. But the issue is that they only told half of the correct facts without clarifying the other, more critical half. This might be worse than saying nothing at all—it's worse than just stating something wrong. . If they don't answer at all, the audience at least knows they don't understand, but by only answering half, the audience might mistakenly think they already understand. If you say something wrong, many will catch it on the spot, but it is hard for the audience to know what you didn't say, or how severely that missing information impacts their perception. Let me lay out the facts: both Taiwanese and imported milk use ultra-high temperature processing. As a result, imported milk lasts 90 days, while Taiwanese milk only lasts 13. But some viewers don't know the full story, and you only answer half of it—saying the shelf lives differ because the pasteurization methods differ. The other. half—that both are ultra-high temperature—is left unsaid. Then viewers fill in the gaps themselves: "Oh, 13 days versus 90 days because of different methods; maybe Taiwanese milk uses low-temperature and imports use high-temperature pasteurization? I get it now, Taiwan is better, it's low-temperature, so I'll buy Taiwanese. " You see, saying only half is worse than saying nothing at all. In the absence of key context, the audience may piece together a wrong answer, and that wrong answer objectively makes domestic milk look better and imports look worse. . Do we really need to take this kind of class? Could it make things worse? That answering only half a question leads the audience to invent wrong answers is not just me making things up. Let me show you the evidence; this is a Sanlih report. >> Usually, the pasteurization temperature for fresh milk is about 70 to 75 degrees . >> Did you hear that? The reporter was comparing fresh milk and shelf-stable milk and stated the 70 to 75-degree pasteurization figure for fresh milk. Are Taiwanese people generally buying milk pasteurized at 70-something degrees ? Is this a case where even the reporter has jumped to a wrong conclusion? Let me show you another one; this is a Liberty Times report from when the controversy. broke out this June and July. It cites the words of Professor Hsu from the Department of Animal Science at NTU. " Taiwan usually uses low-temperature pasteurization to preserve the nutrients in fresh milk." I wonder if the founder is familiar with Professor Hsu? May I ask if the 138 degrees of fresh milk is considered "lower temperature" and better for preserving nutrients compared to Australia's 135 degrees? I believe this was not Professor Hsu's original meaning. The question is, did Liberty Times reporter Yang Yuan-ting check with Professor Hsu before writing this report ? I don't know, but the text literally contains the phrase "Taiwan usually uses.

low-temperature pasteurization." Is this not another example of someone inventing their own facts? PTS Sign Language News is the same. What's more serious is that multiple media outlets have been reporting the wrong facts for so many years. What if this misleads even more consumers? The irony is that this mistake happens to be shared by a domestic milk brand; would the industry have any motivation to step up and admit this error? I actually think it’s really necessary for someone like P to take a look. This kind of issue shouldn't just stay within the dairy circle; it takes a million-subscriber influencer like P to make the topic go viral and be seen by more people. Do you think it’s just. glossing over the fact that Taiwan’s fresh milk is ultra-high temperature processed? No, dodging the temperature issue is where the problem lies. Speaking of pasteurization temperature, it’s not just about shelf life, but also flavor, right? Regarding the claims about nutrition and flavor, there are two problematic points that are even funnier; let’s hear how he answers that . He said that everyone has different ways of pasteurizing, referring to Taiwan’s 13-day milk versus imported milk, then added that refrigeration is needed, there are gaps in flavor and texture, and some people just don’t like the taste of the Maillard reaction. The statement that fresh milk is purer is correct, but it only answers half the question, because Taiwan’s milk is all. ultra-high temperature; if high heat causes a Maillard reaction, then wouldn't brands like Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Fresh Delight, and Lin Feng Ying all have that reaction? Are you saying that Taiwanese people don't like the taste of Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Fresh Delight, and Lin Feng Ying? Comments also mentioned—it seems like an alumnus from the Department of Animal Science at NPUST said—that they remember the dairy processing professor stating it was the Maillard reaction from Taiwan’s ultra-high temperature pasteurization that created the distinct "creamy aroma " in Taiwanese milk; isn't this "creamy aroma" that Taiwanese people love actually the Maillard reaction? If you like Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Fresh Delight, and Lin Feng Ying, isn't it. because they are all ultra-high temperature processed? Why is the Maillard reaction suddenly a bad thing now? Let’s assume there’s an elder who doesn't check the facts, saying: "I like Taiwanese milk because it's pure; I don't drink imported milk because the high heat causes a Maillard reaction, it all tastes burnt." Well, to that elder, when exactly did you taste "pure" Taiwanese milk? Are you drinking Kuang Chuan, Fresh Delight, or Fresh Milk Workshop? Are they all "pure"? Are they using low-temperature pasteurization or high-temperature pasteurization? If it's high-temperature pasteurization, does such high heat cause a burnt aroma from the Maillard reaction, or is it supposed to be fresh and pure? If you like. Taiwanese milk, do you prefer the burnt aroma of the Maillard reaction, or is it supposed to be fresh and pure? This is all so confusing! If you, the audience, are also feeling confused, why don't I ask the questions for you? When placing Taiwanese milk and imported milk side by side, the industry obviously wants us to buy the Taiwanese milk, right? Then why should you choose the Taiwanese milk? Don't talk to me about "Taiwan values"; let's break this down layer by layer. It's about the flavor. If both have Maillard reaction scorched notes and Taiwanese milk is more expensive, why would you choose it? They have to claim they’re different to create a sense of. differentiation. "Taiwanese milk is fresh and pure, imported milk has a scorched Maillard flavor; you like fresh and pure, so you must buy Taiwanese milk ." Doesn't that sound like sound business logic? But I have to ask, Taiwanese milk also undergoes ultra-high temperatures and has those same reactions, so where does this "fresh and pure" come from? "Taiwanese milk is heated to high temperatures, sure, but it only lasts 13 days—the sterilization method is still different.""Look, Taiwan is still a few degrees lower, but the duration is longer—others do one to two seconds, Taiwan does two to five—and the temperature isn't necessarily lower.

Fresh Milk Square is 138 ° C, higher than Australia's 135 ° C. You don't understand, it’s just different."" Taiwanese milk is fresh and pure," yet many tests—and even the industry itself —admit that Taiwanese people like the Maillard reaction flavor, not "fresh and pure." If both have the Maillard reaction, why should I choose the more expensive Taiwanese one? That’s just what you don't know. The Maillard reaction in Taiwanese milk is a "rich, creamy aroma," while in imported milk, it's a "scorched taste." You like the rich, creamy aroma, not the scorched. taste, so you must buy Taiwanese milk. But didn't you say at the beginning that Taiwanese milk was fresh and pure? I poked a hole in their temperature argument, so why the sudden shift to saying it's not fresh and pure? Are the four major brands "pure" because they use low heat, or are they "pure" despite using high heat? Which one is it, exactly? Do you know what it means to be cornered from both sides? This scenario doesn't represent any specific company; it's just a topic you've likely all heard but haven't had the chance to challenge. A flavor is a flavor; it shouldn't be a "rich, creamy aroma" when. it comes from domestic milk and " high-temperature damage" when it comes from imports. Since Taiwanese consumers are already used to—or even enjoy—this processed flavor, why is it that when imported milk uses similar high-heat methods, it's suddenly dismissed as bad-tasting Maillard notes? The founder of Fresh Milk Square must be a professional, right? Surely they know that the milk branded as "fresh" in Taiwan is all ultra-high temperature processed? How can you claim the milk is "pure" when that purity originally belonged to milk pasteurized at 72 degrees? Just because of the term " fresh milk," and because Taiwanese milk has the privilege of using that label,. won't people mistakenly assume that the so-called fresh milk in Taiwan is pasteurized at a low temperature of 72 degrees? No wonder they rushed to amend the law to monopolize the term "fresh milk," so that only Taiwanese milk can use it. If the pure fresh milk you are commenting on is the real, 72-degree pasteurized milk from abroad, it seems reasonable on the surface, but it's not right to say it that way. Can Taiwanese people even get that kind of milk? If you put it that way, won't a bunch of people again think that the mainstream milk in Taiwan is pasteurized at a low temperature of 72 degrees, just like in Europe and America? When answering these. types of questions, don't act as if you're unaware of the actual situation in the Taiwanese market, and don't assume that no one else knows the truth . Because you didn't honestly reveal to the audience the truth that Taiwan also uses ultra-high-temperature pasteurization, you ended up making so many high-minded arguments based on pasteurization temperatures. I don't doubt your expertise, but if the most important facts aren't clarified first, the more you say, the more confused the audience will be, and the further they will drift from the truth. Regarding the two previous questions about shelf life and flavor, I honestly don't know if the two hosts are aware that Taiwan uses ultra-high temperatures. When you ask these questions, do you have this. picture in your mind? Imported milk is ultra-high temperature, and Taiwanese milk is also ultra-high temperature. Of course, I don't know if the two hosts are aware of this reality, but if they were, they probably wouldn't let the industry representative answer like that , right? Normally, one would continue to press them; they shouldn't have been able to dodge the question so smoothly. There are three aspects affected by pasteurization temperature: low pasteurization temperature means a shorter shelf life, better flavor, and less nutrient loss. When a bottle of milk is true fresh milk—the kind of 72- degree low-temperature pasteurized fresh milk found in Europe and America—the above three points are fine. But when people in Taiwan mistakenly believe that.

local fresh milk is all pasteurized at that lower 72-degree temperature, all three points become very problematic. Let's look at where the male host asked a good question, one that hit the nail on the head. For example, when discussing the pasteurization temperature of fresh milk, he asked, " Is there a difference in nutritional value?" The founder replied that there would be some gaps and more B-vitamin loss. Here comes the key point: the host followed up by asking, "Is this slight loss significant enough to impact human health?" The founder answered that, basically, he didn't think it would have a significant impact; even Professor Chen Ming-ru from NTU said there was almost no difference. Isn't it much. better to ask it this way? Let's first commend the male host for being willing to follow up on whether nutritional loss makes a difference. This is already quite sharp, effectively forcing them to admit there's almost no nutritional difference. It's a wake-up call for the older generation who pay the highest prices in the world for Taiwanese milk, believing imported milk loses nutrients while local milk retains them. I don't know if this will wake them up, but the question the male host asked doesn't hold up, as I just mentioned regarding shelf life, flavor, and nutrition. The discussion of these three points only makes sense if we assume Taiwanese milk is pasteurized at 72 degrees and. imported milk at 135 degrees; only then is there a comparison worth making. The fact is, both Taiwanese and imported milk undergo ultra-high temperature processing, so insisting there’s a difference in shelf life, flavor, and nutrition is just bizarre. The answer extracted from the industry suggests that while low-temperature pasteurization retains nutrients, high-temperature pasteurization doesn't cause significant loss either, so there’s almost no nutritional difference between them. Some older folks previously thought Taiwanese milk was more nutritious due to low-temperature processing, but it turns out that the nutritional advantage isn't that significant. The industry provided some accurate information, such as discussing. vitamins and protein denaturation, but as I said at the start, telling only half the story is worse than not answering at all. The part they didn't say is more important: that Taiwanese milk is also high-temperature, not low-temperature. How about I follow up with the half they didn't mention? I won't talk to you about nutritional expertise; I'll just follow your own logic. If your milk is treated at 138 degrees (plus or minus two) for 1.5 to 2 seconds, does it actually lose fewer vitamins than Australian long-life milk treated at 135 degrees for 1 to 2 seconds? Does your protein undergo less denaturation compared to Kirkland milk. treated at 138 degrees for two seconds? Hosts, why don't you ask it like that? When everyone is unaware of the actual pasteurization temperatures, talking about vitamins and whey protein sounds very professional. But when the pasteurization temperatures are exposed to the light of day, if you still want to claim Taiwanese milk loses fewer nutrients, you have to explain how your higher temperature somehow results in less loss. And if you don't claim Taiwanese milk loses less, it implies high temperatures don't cause nutrient loss, meaning there's no difference between Taiwanese and imported milk. Consumers will then wonder: "It makes no. difference, so why should I buy the most expensive Taiwanese milk in the world?" If someone still insists that " nutrition isn't completely preserved, vitamins B and C might have a 7%to 8% loss, and whey protein might denature," then I have to ask: if imported milk's vitamins and proteins lose some value, doesn't Taiwanese milk lose them too? Moreover, vitamins like ferritin are not the primary nutrients, so the host at least asked a good question: "Is this minor loss really that important?" Of course not. Otherwise, what would people who don't drink milk do? I know some people will still insist that Taiwanese.

milk uses a lower temperature—125 to 135 degrees—and compared to 135 degrees, it has a fresher flavor and preserves more nutrients. So, I will just ask a question that any elementary school student could answer. Ignoring the 138- degree milk from Xianrufang for a moment , we have three levels: 72 degrees, 125 to 135 degrees, and 135 degrees. Between these, is the 125-135 degree range closer to 72 degrees or 135 degrees? >> Well, answer me. >> Is the flavor and nutrition of this 125-135 degree Taiwanese milk closer to 72-degree milk? Or is it closer to 135-. degree imported milk? That is why I say this is an elementary school question. Let’s look at somatic cell counts. Somatic cells are not pathogens, nor are they a food standard. They primarily reflect the health of the cow's udder and are an indicator of raw milk quality . The fewer there are, the healthier the udder, so fewer somatic cells mean better milk. But this is where it gets strange: they claim Taiwan’s Grade A milk standard is under 300,000 cells. Then they immediately mention that the U.S. allows up to 750,000 for Grade A, implying their standards are looser. The founder of Xianrufang should be an expert, right? They should know more. than the average person and think more logically, right? The legal maximum doesn't equal the actual value. Just because the passing grade is 60 doesn't mean you always score a 60. Didn't the Dairy Association just claim this July that all Taiwanese milk is Grade A while foreign milk is lower grade? The reasoning is the same as in the video: Taiwan is Grade A under 300,000, while the U.S. is Grade A up to 750,000. They use the legal limit to imply that others are inferior based on looser standards. You all should know how much controversy that caused at the time. Didn't Kelly also say on the show that Japanese milk for kids is, um...Well, according to the. Dairy Association's logic, that would be second-rate milk. Founder of Xianrufang , the Dairy Association already said this back then, and now you are saying it again. Let me show you the data. Taiwan only publishes data up to the county level; 190,000 in 2024 is lower than 300,000, so it is Grade A. But what about the U.S.? It was 171,000 in 2023 and 169,000 in 2022. Is 170,000 lower than 190,000? And what about New Zealand ? 157,000. Is 157,000 not lower than Kuang Chuan's 190,000? I'll show you the image directly. The somatic cell counts. from the industry association and the union are both higher than the US figures they cited themselves. So, you can't imply others are worse or you are better just because their standards are looser, because the actual data in Taiwan isn't necessarily better. If Class A has a passing grade of 60 and Class B has a passing grade of 70, does having a higher standard mean Class B is better than Class A? It could be that everyone in Class A scores 100 or 98, while those in Class B just barely pass with 70 or 80. Kuang Chuan is one of the few willing to disclose data, but what about those who haven't? Are their somatic cell counts lower or higher than Kuang Chuan's? According to Taiwan data. cited by the USDA, Taiwan's count was 214,000 in 2022. How can you just equate standards with quality! This is just like what I said before: everything stated is professional and factual, but telling only half the truth is worse than saying nothing at all, especially when the other half could completely overturn your perception. Bai-Guo, why didn't you take the opportunity to ask if they know what the somatic cell counts are in the US or New Zealand? And what is the somatic cell count of Xian-Lu-Fang itself? Of course, if Xian-Lu-Fang's somatic cell count is lower than New Zealand's 157,000, then they're truly impressive. But logically speaking, you cannot simply use.

standards as a proxy for quality to prove that Taiwan is better than other countries. Next, he says the US can use bovine growth hormones while Taiwan cannot. I won't shy away from the facts —the US does use growth hormones—but he didn't mention that the EU and New Zealand also prohibit them. So, don't group the US with other imports just because Taiwan can't use them but the US can. Does the fact that the US can use growth hormones mean everyone is using them? USDA data shows that in 2000, about 17%of dairy farms used growth hormones, but by 2021, it was down to. about 1%. In terms of milk production, milk from farms using growth hormones dropped from 40%in 2005 to 2%in 2021. The use of growth hormones has plummeted year by year. Requirements from large retail chains like Walmart and dairy processors have made milk produced with growth hormones increasingly unpopular. Plus, with limited benefits, growth hormones are gradually losing their market appeal in the US dairy industry. Note this: just because it's not legally banned in the US doesn't mean everyone is still using it. So, as you can see, it's the same as the somatic cell issue —only half the story is being told. Others have looser standards, but they. don't tell you that Taiwan has strict standards in name only, while reality isn't actually better. They just cite U.S. regulations without mentioning they're rarely used now. They skip what should be said, yet they're happy to talk about what shouldn't be! They claim U.S. growth hormones are just like ractopamine, but they differ in physiological effects, usage, and purpose—you simply can't compare them. They omit facts favorable to imported milk while thoroughly detailing things unfavorable to imports to lead you to certain conclusions. I didn't hide that the U.S. allows growth hormones, nor am I defending the U.S. dairy industry, but. you can't distort the facts. And there's another point I've repeated time and again: imported milk is not just "ice brick"(frozen concentrate) milk. For instance, they say if it's reconstituted milk, the ingredients are more complex, so you have to check the back label. May I ask, reconstituted milk refers to ice brick milk mixed with water, right? It’s true that ice brick milk allows for some electrolyte additives, but the way you say "check the back label" is misleading . Aren't ice brick milk products exclusively for commercial use? Can general consumers even buy commercial. milk at retail stores? When you say "check the back label," don't you think people might mistakenly believe all imports are ice bricks that need checking? Of course not; what's sold directly in retail stores is 100% pure milk. Of course, reconstituted milk isn't just ice bricks; it also includes milk powder. You said to check the back label, right? Are you sure? I checked, and this is Kuang Chuan fruit milk—it contains milk powder! So, local Taiwanese brands also use reconstituted milk? Is this what you meant by telling us to check the back label? Since Taiwan. isn't naturally suited for dairy farming , some ask why we don't just follow Singapore and Hong Kong and import everything. Singapore's protein self-sufficiency rate was affected by pandemic import/export disruptions, so they plan to raise it to 30%by 2030. But people are asking about milk, not general protein—what does importing all our milk have to do with protein rates? If there's suddenly no milk, we can use other proteins. The point is, milk isn't suitable for local production, so why not import everything like Singapore? Does a high protein rate require us to.

force domestic milk production? And like this comment says, "Just in case, Taiwan would still have milk to drink." But as the founder of a local dairy brand and industry insiders have pointed out, all the feed for Taiwan's dairy cows is imported! If the worst were to happen, you’d be out of feed too. Is Taiwan’s high self-sufficiency rate for milk even real? Isn't it just keeping import shares low through protectionist quotas ? Is this just to maintain the sky-high prices of domestic milk? If we're talking about protein self-sufficiency and nutrition, the Health Promotion Administration states that Taiwanese people consume insufficient dairy—only half of what people in the West do, or even less. So, is Taiwan raising self-sufficiency for the sake of public. health? Not at all. With the current supply shortage, do you know what the Taiwanese dairy industry is doing? They’re cutting production and planning to cull dairy cows. When people don't even have enough milk to drink, they’re cutting supply. Does that look like an attempt to boost self-sufficiency? Self-sufficiency is a fake issue; we import all our feed. If there were a naval blockade, where would that self-sufficiency be? I want to ask: if you think dairy is a staple like rice or wheat, shouldn't the government regulate its price? Shouldn't they be ensuring the supply volume? Then why let Taiwanese milk become the most expensive in the world, or even create trade. barriers through legislation? They even use programs like "Classroom Milk" to treat students like recycling bins, making them drink it to clear out inventory. If dairy is truly an essential good, we should ensure supply instead of cutting production when per capita intake is already low. We should make prices reasonable and bring down those sky-high costs, rather than playing games to maintain them. If you claim to believe in market mechanisms, don't push farmers out whenever New Zealand is mentioned. You can't demand market mechanisms when selling for a high price, then beg for protection when it's time to compete. Didn't you say you. wanted market mechanisms? If we're talking market mechanisms, let the inefficient fail. How can you claim there's a market mechanism with so many protectionist measures? Wheat is a vital food source and we import that freely without worrying about a blockade cutting off our noodles. So why protect dairy—which is practically a luxury item in Taiwan—and hide behind farmers? Stop using "local" and "fresh" as an excuse to play the victim. After electronic watches arrived, they outperformed mechanical watches in value, so mechanical watches pivoted to luxury. When ballpoint pens arrived, they outperformed fountain pens, so fountain pens went luxury. If domestic milk can't compete in commercial scale or if its. technology is behind global standards, it should definitely pivot toward premium or high-quality development, just like mechanical watches. But you've stated that this is a staple commodity and a daily necessity. I don't oppose local milk brands focusing on their specialty, but they should just remain niche specialty brands. If a premium milk brand thinks those with deep pockets should buy them, it's like the wheat in Daya, Taichung. Surely not everyone needs to produce luxury boutique products, right? You can't make all cars unaffordable for the average person; there must be cheaper options available as well. Taiwanese milk should take a backseat and stay niche, like supercars; whoever wants to splurge can buy them, but the mass market should be. dominated by imported milk. This means Taiwan could import millions of tons of milk from the US and New Zealand annually, but right now, locally produced milk accounts for 90%, and they’re all obsessed with emphasizing their "specialty." Is it really necessary to block all Taiwanese people from the opportunity to buy milk at a reasonable price just for this? If every brand ends up doing this, then can we still really call milk a necessity? Thankfully, wheat is almost entirely imported; otherwise, all your flour-based foods would cost three or four times more right now. y.

=============

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUqJ2OBfB6s

百靈果《The KK Show 387》邀請鮮乳坊創辦人阿嘉，討論為什麼台灣牛奶比日本貴，以及台灣乳業與進口牛奶的差異。

但訪談中提到的體細胞數（SCC）、美國乳源標準、牛隻生長激素（rbST）、牛奶殺菌方式、營養與保存期限，真的足以證明台灣牛奶比進口牛奶更好嗎？

這支影片針對該集訪談內容進行資料查核與評論，補上幾個容易被忽略的關鍵問題：

本片討論重點

item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUqJ2OBfB6s

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開台灣國產鮮乳與進口鮮乳保存期限巨大差異背後的真正原因。
  • 釐清大眾及主流媒體長年誤將台灣鮮乳視為「低溫殺菌」的認知盲區與事實真相。
  • 深入分析業界代表在訪談中「只說一半實話」如何無形中誤導消費者對風味與品質的判斷。

摘要

百靈果專訪鮮乳坊引發的保存期爭議

作者指出，知名Podcast節目《百靈果》在專訪鮮乳坊創辦人時，主持人凱莉提出了一個民眾普遍好奇的核心疑問：為何台灣鮮乳的保存期限通常只有約十三天，而進口鮮乳卻能保存三十天甚至八、九十天？面對該提問，受訪者僅表示國外也有短效期的鮮乳、不同殺菌方式會影響保存期限與口感，並提及梅納反應對風味的影響，卻始終未正面解釋關鍵的差異本質，令許多期待聽到真相的觀眾感到受訪者在刻意迴避。

台灣鮮乳普遍採用超高溫殺菌的真相

作者進一步強調，一般民眾容易誤以為台灣鮮乳之所以保存期限短，是因為採用了歐美常見的72度低溫巴氏殺菌；但事實上，農業數據與消基會資料均證實，台灣高達99%的鮮乳都是採用125度至138度的超高溫滅菌（UHT）技術。國產鮮乳與進口乳在殺菌溫度上並無顯著較低，甚至殺菌溫度可能更高，然而台灣鮮乳卻只能冷藏保存不到兩週。作者質疑，這其中的關鍵其實是無菌充填技術與保存條件，受訪者卻將問題歸咎於殺菌溫度差異，完全偏離了核心事實。

只說一半的實話對消費者認知的誤導

作者認為，在訪談中「只說一半的實話」比說錯話更為嚴重，因為缺少關鍵資訊會導致觀眾自行腦補錯誤結論，甚至連主流媒體記者都長年誤報台灣鮮乳是低溫殺菌。此外，受訪者稱進口乳因高溫產生梅納反應而風味不如鮮乳純淨，但事實上台灣各大品牌同樣採用超高溫殺菌，若依此邏輯也會產生梅納反應。作者呼籲乳品產業應公開透明地呈現完整科學事實，而非利用資訊落差與避重就輕的話術誤導消費者對國產鮮乳與進口乳的認知。

================================================

The Bailingguo podcast invited the founder of Milk Man; this interview is incredibly packed with insights. For instance, Kylie asked, "Why does Taiwanese fresh milk expire so quickly? ""Foreign milk can last for 30 days." Anyone who knows the truth about Taiwan’s fresh milk must think that was a great question, right? So satisfying! Asking him directly to his face to see how he’d answer—yeah, why is that? The comments section also felt it hit the nail on the head, but naturally, he didn't really answer it; he just dodged the question. For those of you who know the truth, let's not spoil it yet. For viewers watching on a computer, I suggest opening the original interview video as well and checking each segment along the timeline; if the original. makes you want to roll your eyes, you can come back here to see how he actually responded. He said that abroad there is also shorter-shelf-life milk, that everyone uses different sterilization methods, and with Taiwan's current methods, it's about two weeks and must be refrigerated; there’s a difference in flavor and texture, and some people don't like the Maillard reaction taste, so [his] fresh milk is purer. It looks like he answered it, right? Different shelf lives because domestic and foreign sterilization methods differ, but that’s not what the audience wants to know. "Everyone uses different sterilization methods"—who is "everyone"? When you say "different," who exactly is being compared to whom? You replied that there is also short-shelf-life milk abroad, usually at 72 to 75 degrees for 15 seconds, sold locally for quick consumption; that statement itself isn't wrong, but what Kylie was asking about was the imported milk we see in Taiwan—why is its shelf life longer? Now, can I be the one to ask? Hitting the nail on the head isn't enough; we need to cut to the bone and ask who is being compared to whom: when Taiwan's Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Richi, Lin Fengying, or even your Milk Man, are compared to American imports like Costco’s Kirkland or Foremost, why can theirs last 85 or 90 days while. Taiwan's only lasts 13? "Different sterilization methods"—how, exactly, are they different? When viewers see that Taiwan's fresh milk only lasts 13 days, might they think it's the same 72- degree low-temperature pasteurization used locally in Europe and America? How innocent, how kind—so it's different from the ultra-high temperature used for imported milk? The truth is, Taiwan's fresh milk is all ultra-high temperature ! Isn't the agricultural data right here ? 99%is UHT; the Consumers 'Foundation also says Taiwanese milk is basically long-life milk, 125 to 135 degrees, while imported milk is 135 or 138 degrees—how many degrees lower is that,. really? So is*this*what you meant by " different"? Let's look at the dairy industry: 138 degrees for 1.5 to 2 seconds, yet it only lasts 13 days refrigerated. Australian UHT milk is 135 degrees for 1 to 2 seconds and can be stored at room temperature for 12 months . Yes, the sterilization methods are different. Domestic milk is three degrees higher than imported milk. It's different, but because it's at a higher temperature, the shelf life is actually shorter? Is that how it works? Or is it because there's no aseptic filling? Although some comments felt it was spot on, others felt the guest was shifting the focus and dodging questions, only saying what they wanted to say. Look,. they addressed the previous sentence about fresh milk quite directly, then immediately switched to other topics, starting to talk about raw milk consumption in the US fitness community . So, what about the sterilization temperature and shelf life that everyone wanted to know about? Dodged. They didn't answer. That's why the audience feels like vomiting blood watching this . I'm not taking things out of context. Seriously, the timeline is down below; you can all go back and check the original video. The female host's complete question should have been, " Taiwan uses such high temperatures of over 130 degrees for sterilization, so why can it still only last 13 days?" Your dairy products are at 138 degrees, plus or minus two. This temperature is.

even higher than many in Europe and America, so why is it still only 13 days ? If you only intended for it to last 13 days anyway, why use such a high temperature? Pasteurization at 72 degrees lasts 13 days, and sterilization at 138 degrees still only lasts 13 days , so wasn't that high heat for nothing? If you asked that on the spot, let's see how they could dodge it! Exactly, why didn't they press them for an answer? Everyone wanted to hear it. Right, if the local sentiment in Taiwan is really like that, and so many people truly don't know that Taiwan's fresh milk uses ultra-high heat, mistakenly believing it's low-temperature and pure, no wonder the industry is desperate to amend the law to monopolize the term "fresh milk" for domestic use only. So why does the audience feel like vomiting blood? At that moment, you just want to smash the screen and jump in to ask yourself. There was even a comment telling me to come and take a class. I guess the implication is that I don't understand milk, I just don't know how to say Taiwan's fresh milk is the best in the world. Let me take a step back and explain where the problem with this interview lies. It's not that what the industry representatives said was wrong ; much of the knowledge is professional when taken in isolation. But the issue is that they only told half of the correct facts without clarifying the other, more critical half. This might be worse than saying nothing at all—it's worse than just stating something wrong. . If they don't answer at all, the audience at least knows they don't understand, but by only answering half, the audience might mistakenly think they already understand. If you say something wrong, many will catch it on the spot, but it is hard for the audience to know what you didn't say, or how severely that missing information impacts their perception. Let me lay out the facts: both Taiwanese and imported milk use ultra-high temperature processing. As a result, imported milk lasts 90 days, while Taiwanese milk only lasts 13. But some viewers don't know the full story, and you only answer half of it—saying the shelf lives differ because the pasteurization methods differ. The other. half—that both are ultra-high temperature—is left unsaid. Then viewers fill in the gaps themselves: "Oh, 13 days versus 90 days because of different methods; maybe Taiwanese milk uses low-temperature and imports use high-temperature pasteurization? I get it now, Taiwan is better, it's low-temperature, so I'll buy Taiwanese. " You see, saying only half is worse than saying nothing at all. In the absence of key context, the audience may piece together a wrong answer, and that wrong answer objectively makes domestic milk look better and imports look worse. . Do we really need to take this kind of class? Could it make things worse? That answering only half a question leads the audience to invent wrong answers is not just me making things up. Let me show you the evidence; this is a Sanlih report. >> Usually, the pasteurization temperature for fresh milk is about 70 to 75 degrees . >> Did you hear that? The reporter was comparing fresh milk and shelf-stable milk and stated the 70 to 75-degree pasteurization figure for fresh milk. Are Taiwanese people generally buying milk pasteurized at 70-something degrees ? Is this a case where even the reporter has jumped to a wrong conclusion? Let me show you another one; this is a Liberty Times report from when the controversy. broke out this June and July. It cites the words of Professor Hsu from the Department of Animal Science at NTU. " Taiwan usually uses low-temperature pasteurization to preserve the nutrients in fresh milk." I wonder if the founder is familiar with Professor Hsu? May I ask if the 138 degrees of fresh milk is considered "lower temperature" and better for preserving nutrients compared to Australia's 135 degrees? I believe this was not Professor Hsu's original meaning. The question is, did Liberty Times reporter Yang Yuan-ting check with Professor Hsu before writing this report ? I don't know, but the text literally contains the phrase "Taiwan usually uses.

low-temperature pasteurization." Is this not another example of someone inventing their own facts? PTS Sign Language News is the same. What's more serious is that multiple media outlets have been reporting the wrong facts for so many years. What if this misleads even more consumers? The irony is that this mistake happens to be shared by a domestic milk brand; would the industry have any motivation to step up and admit this error? I actually think it’s really necessary for someone like P to take a look. This kind of issue shouldn't just stay within the dairy circle; it takes a million-subscriber influencer like P to make the topic go viral and be seen by more people. Do you think it’s just. glossing over the fact that Taiwan’s fresh milk is ultra-high temperature processed? No, dodging the temperature issue is where the problem lies. Speaking of pasteurization temperature, it’s not just about shelf life, but also flavor, right? Regarding the claims about nutrition and flavor, there are two problematic points that are even funnier; let’s hear how he answers that . He said that everyone has different ways of pasteurizing, referring to Taiwan’s 13-day milk versus imported milk, then added that refrigeration is needed, there are gaps in flavor and texture, and some people just don’t like the taste of the Maillard reaction. The statement that fresh milk is purer is correct, but it only answers half the question, because Taiwan’s milk is all. ultra-high temperature; if high heat causes a Maillard reaction, then wouldn't brands like Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Fresh Delight, and Lin Feng Ying all have that reaction? Are you saying that Taiwanese people don't like the taste of Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Fresh Delight, and Lin Feng Ying? Comments also mentioned—it seems like an alumnus from the Department of Animal Science at NPUST said—that they remember the dairy processing professor stating it was the Maillard reaction from Taiwan’s ultra-high temperature pasteurization that created the distinct "creamy aroma " in Taiwanese milk; isn't this "creamy aroma" that Taiwanese people love actually the Maillard reaction? If you like Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Fresh Delight, and Lin Feng Ying, isn't it. because they are all ultra-high temperature processed? Why is the Maillard reaction suddenly a bad thing now? Let’s assume there’s an elder who doesn't check the facts, saying: "I like Taiwanese milk because it's pure; I don't drink imported milk because the high heat causes a Maillard reaction, it all tastes burnt." Well, to that elder, when exactly did you taste "pure" Taiwanese milk? Are you drinking Kuang Chuan, Fresh Delight, or Fresh Milk Workshop? Are they all "pure"? Are they using low-temperature pasteurization or high-temperature pasteurization? If it's high-temperature pasteurization, does such high heat cause a burnt aroma from the Maillard reaction, or is it supposed to be fresh and pure? If you like. Taiwanese milk, do you prefer the burnt aroma of the Maillard reaction, or is it supposed to be fresh and pure? This is all so confusing! If you, the audience, are also feeling confused, why don't I ask the questions for you? When placing Taiwanese milk and imported milk side by side, the industry obviously wants us to buy the Taiwanese milk, right? Then why should you choose the Taiwanese milk? Don't talk to me about "Taiwan values"; let's break this down layer by layer. It's about the flavor. If both have Maillard reaction scorched notes and Taiwanese milk is more expensive, why would you choose it? They have to claim they’re different to create a sense of. differentiation. "Taiwanese milk is fresh and pure, imported milk has a scorched Maillard flavor; you like fresh and pure, so you must buy Taiwanese milk ." Doesn't that sound like sound business logic? But I have to ask, Taiwanese milk also undergoes ultra-high temperatures and has those same reactions, so where does this "fresh and pure" come from? "Taiwanese milk is heated to high temperatures, sure, but it only lasts 13 days—the sterilization method is still different.""Look, Taiwan is still a few degrees lower, but the duration is longer—others do one to two seconds, Taiwan does two to five—and the temperature isn't necessarily lower.

Fresh Milk Square is 138 ° C, higher than Australia's 135 ° C. You don't understand, it’s just different."" Taiwanese milk is fresh and pure," yet many tests—and even the industry itself —admit that Taiwanese people like the Maillard reaction flavor, not "fresh and pure." If both have the Maillard reaction, why should I choose the more expensive Taiwanese one? That’s just what you don't know. The Maillard reaction in Taiwanese milk is a "rich, creamy aroma," while in imported milk, it's a "scorched taste." You like the rich, creamy aroma, not the scorched. taste, so you must buy Taiwanese milk. But didn't you say at the beginning that Taiwanese milk was fresh and pure? I poked a hole in their temperature argument, so why the sudden shift to saying it's not fresh and pure? Are the four major brands "pure" because they use low heat, or are they "pure" despite using high heat? Which one is it, exactly? Do you know what it means to be cornered from both sides? This scenario doesn't represent any specific company; it's just a topic you've likely all heard but haven't had the chance to challenge. A flavor is a flavor; it shouldn't be a "rich, creamy aroma" when. it comes from domestic milk and " high-temperature damage" when it comes from imports. Since Taiwanese consumers are already used to—or even enjoy—this processed flavor, why is it that when imported milk uses similar high-heat methods, it's suddenly dismissed as bad-tasting Maillard notes? The founder of Fresh Milk Square must be a professional, right? Surely they know that the milk branded as "fresh" in Taiwan is all ultra-high temperature processed? How can you claim the milk is "pure" when that purity originally belonged to milk pasteurized at 72 degrees? Just because of the term " fresh milk," and because Taiwanese milk has the privilege of using that label,. won't people mistakenly assume that the so-called fresh milk in Taiwan is pasteurized at a low temperature of 72 degrees? No wonder they rushed to amend the law to monopolize the term "fresh milk," so that only Taiwanese milk can use it. If the pure fresh milk you are commenting on is the real, 72-degree pasteurized milk from abroad, it seems reasonable on the surface, but it's not right to say it that way. Can Taiwanese people even get that kind of milk? If you put it that way, won't a bunch of people again think that the mainstream milk in Taiwan is pasteurized at a low temperature of 72 degrees, just like in Europe and America? When answering these. types of questions, don't act as if you're unaware of the actual situation in the Taiwanese market, and don't assume that no one else knows the truth . Because you didn't honestly reveal to the audience the truth that Taiwan also uses ultra-high-temperature pasteurization, you ended up making so many high-minded arguments based on pasteurization temperatures. I don't doubt your expertise, but if the most important facts aren't clarified first, the more you say, the more confused the audience will be, and the further they will drift from the truth. Regarding the two previous questions about shelf life and flavor, I honestly don't know if the two hosts are aware that Taiwan uses ultra-high temperatures. When you ask these questions, do you have this. picture in your mind? Imported milk is ultra-high temperature, and Taiwanese milk is also ultra-high temperature. Of course, I don't know if the two hosts are aware of this reality, but if they were, they probably wouldn't let the industry representative answer like that , right? Normally, one would continue to press them; they shouldn't have been able to dodge the question so smoothly. There are three aspects affected by pasteurization temperature: low pasteurization temperature means a shorter shelf life, better flavor, and less nutrient loss. When a bottle of milk is true fresh milk—the kind of 72- degree low-temperature pasteurized fresh milk found in Europe and America—the above three points are fine. But when people in Taiwan mistakenly believe that.

local fresh milk is all pasteurized at that lower 72-degree temperature, all three points become very problematic. Let's look at where the male host asked a good question, one that hit the nail on the head. For example, when discussing the pasteurization temperature of fresh milk, he asked, " Is there a difference in nutritional value?" The founder replied that there would be some gaps and more B-vitamin loss. Here comes the key point: the host followed up by asking, "Is this slight loss significant enough to impact human health?" The founder answered that, basically, he didn't think it would have a significant impact; even Professor Chen Ming-ru from NTU said there was almost no difference. Isn't it much. better to ask it this way? Let's first commend the male host for being willing to follow up on whether nutritional loss makes a difference. This is already quite sharp, effectively forcing them to admit there's almost no nutritional difference. It's a wake-up call for the older generation who pay the highest prices in the world for Taiwanese milk, believing imported milk loses nutrients while local milk retains them. I don't know if this will wake them up, but the question the male host asked doesn't hold up, as I just mentioned regarding shelf life, flavor, and nutrition. The discussion of these three points only makes sense if we assume Taiwanese milk is pasteurized at 72 degrees and. imported milk at 135 degrees; only then is there a comparison worth making. The fact is, both Taiwanese and imported milk undergo ultra-high temperature processing, so insisting there’s a difference in shelf life, flavor, and nutrition is just bizarre. The answer extracted from the industry suggests that while low-temperature pasteurization retains nutrients, high-temperature pasteurization doesn't cause significant loss either, so there’s almost no nutritional difference between them. Some older folks previously thought Taiwanese milk was more nutritious due to low-temperature processing, but it turns out that the nutritional advantage isn't that significant. The industry provided some accurate information, such as discussing. vitamins and protein denaturation, but as I said at the start, telling only half the story is worse than not answering at all. The part they didn't say is more important: that Taiwanese milk is also high-temperature, not low-temperature. How about I follow up with the half they didn't mention? I won't talk to you about nutritional expertise; I'll just follow your own logic. If your milk is treated at 138 degrees (plus or minus two) for 1.5 to 2 seconds, does it actually lose fewer vitamins than Australian long-life milk treated at 135 degrees for 1 to 2 seconds? Does your protein undergo less denaturation compared to Kirkland milk. treated at 138 degrees for two seconds? Hosts, why don't you ask it like that? When everyone is unaware of the actual pasteurization temperatures, talking about vitamins and whey protein sounds very professional. But when the pasteurization temperatures are exposed to the light of day, if you still want to claim Taiwanese milk loses fewer nutrients, you have to explain how your higher temperature somehow results in less loss. And if you don't claim Taiwanese milk loses less, it implies high temperatures don't cause nutrient loss, meaning there's no difference between Taiwanese and imported milk. Consumers will then wonder: "It makes no. difference, so why should I buy the most expensive Taiwanese milk in the world?" If someone still insists that " nutrition isn't completely preserved, vitamins B and C might have a 7%to 8% loss, and whey protein might denature," then I have to ask: if imported milk's vitamins and proteins lose some value, doesn't Taiwanese milk lose them too? Moreover, vitamins like ferritin are not the primary nutrients, so the host at least asked a good question: "Is this minor loss really that important?" Of course not. Otherwise, what would people who don't drink milk do? I know some people will still insist that Taiwanese.

milk uses a lower temperature—125 to 135 degrees—and compared to 135 degrees, it has a fresher flavor and preserves more nutrients. So, I will just ask a question that any elementary school student could answer. Ignoring the 138- degree milk from Xianrufang for a moment , we have three levels: 72 degrees, 125 to 135 degrees, and 135 degrees. Between these, is the 125-135 degree range closer to 72 degrees or 135 degrees? >> Well, answer me. >> Is the flavor and nutrition of this 125-135 degree Taiwanese milk closer to 72-degree milk? Or is it closer to 135-. degree imported milk? That is why I say this is an elementary school question. Let’s look at somatic cell counts. Somatic cells are not pathogens, nor are they a food standard. They primarily reflect the health of the cow's udder and are an indicator of raw milk quality . The fewer there are, the healthier the udder, so fewer somatic cells mean better milk. But this is where it gets strange: they claim Taiwan’s Grade A milk standard is under 300,000 cells. Then they immediately mention that the U.S. allows up to 750,000 for Grade A, implying their standards are looser. The founder of Xianrufang should be an expert, right? They should know more. than the average person and think more logically, right? The legal maximum doesn't equal the actual value. Just because the passing grade is 60 doesn't mean you always score a 60. Didn't the Dairy Association just claim this July that all Taiwanese milk is Grade A while foreign milk is lower grade? The reasoning is the same as in the video: Taiwan is Grade A under 300,000, while the U.S. is Grade A up to 750,000. They use the legal limit to imply that others are inferior based on looser standards. You all should know how much controversy that caused at the time. Didn't Kelly also say on the show that Japanese milk for kids is, um...Well, according to the. Dairy Association's logic, that would be second-rate milk. Founder of Xianrufang , the Dairy Association already said this back then, and now you are saying it again. Let me show you the data. Taiwan only publishes data up to the county level; 190,000 in 2024 is lower than 300,000, so it is Grade A. But what about the U.S.? It was 171,000 in 2023 and 169,000 in 2022. Is 170,000 lower than 190,000? And what about New Zealand ? 157,000. Is 157,000 not lower than Kuang Chuan's 190,000? I'll show you the image directly. The somatic cell counts. from the industry association and the union are both higher than the US figures they cited themselves. So, you can't imply others are worse or you are better just because their standards are looser, because the actual data in Taiwan isn't necessarily better. If Class A has a passing grade of 60 and Class B has a passing grade of 70, does having a higher standard mean Class B is better than Class A? It could be that everyone in Class A scores 100 or 98, while those in Class B just barely pass with 70 or 80. Kuang Chuan is one of the few willing to disclose data, but what about those who haven't? Are their somatic cell counts lower or higher than Kuang Chuan's? According to Taiwan data. cited by the USDA, Taiwan's count was 214,000 in 2022. How can you just equate standards with quality! This is just like what I said before: everything stated is professional and factual, but telling only half the truth is worse than saying nothing at all, especially when the other half could completely overturn your perception. Bai-Guo, why didn't you take the opportunity to ask if they know what the somatic cell counts are in the US or New Zealand? And what is the somatic cell count of Xian-Lu-Fang itself? Of course, if Xian-Lu-Fang's somatic cell count is lower than New Zealand's 157,000, then they're truly impressive. But logically speaking, you cannot simply use.

standards as a proxy for quality to prove that Taiwan is better than other countries. Next, he says the US can use bovine growth hormones while Taiwan cannot. I won't shy away from the facts —the US does use growth hormones—but he didn't mention that the EU and New Zealand also prohibit them. So, don't group the US with other imports just because Taiwan can't use them but the US can. Does the fact that the US can use growth hormones mean everyone is using them? USDA data shows that in 2000, about 17%of dairy farms used growth hormones, but by 2021, it was down to. about 1%. In terms of milk production, milk from farms using growth hormones dropped from 40%in 2005 to 2%in 2021. The use of growth hormones has plummeted year by year. Requirements from large retail chains like Walmart and dairy processors have made milk produced with growth hormones increasingly unpopular. Plus, with limited benefits, growth hormones are gradually losing their market appeal in the US dairy industry. Note this: just because it's not legally banned in the US doesn't mean everyone is still using it. So, as you can see, it's the same as the somatic cell issue —only half the story is being told. Others have looser standards, but they. don't tell you that Taiwan has strict standards in name only, while reality isn't actually better. They just cite U.S. regulations without mentioning they're rarely used now. They skip what should be said, yet they're happy to talk about what shouldn't be! They claim U.S. growth hormones are just like ractopamine, but they differ in physiological effects, usage, and purpose—you simply can't compare them. They omit facts favorable to imported milk while thoroughly detailing things unfavorable to imports to lead you to certain conclusions. I didn't hide that the U.S. allows growth hormones, nor am I defending the U.S. dairy industry, but. you can't distort the facts. And there's another point I've repeated time and again: imported milk is not just "ice brick"(frozen concentrate) milk. For instance, they say if it's reconstituted milk, the ingredients are more complex, so you have to check the back label. May I ask, reconstituted milk refers to ice brick milk mixed with water, right? It’s true that ice brick milk allows for some electrolyte additives, but the way you say "check the back label" is misleading . Aren't ice brick milk products exclusively for commercial use? Can general consumers even buy commercial. milk at retail stores? When you say "check the back label," don't you think people might mistakenly believe all imports are ice bricks that need checking? Of course not; what's sold directly in retail stores is 100% pure milk. Of course, reconstituted milk isn't just ice bricks; it also includes milk powder. You said to check the back label, right? Are you sure? I checked, and this is Kuang Chuan fruit milk—it contains milk powder! So, local Taiwanese brands also use reconstituted milk? Is this what you meant by telling us to check the back label? Since Taiwan. isn't naturally suited for dairy farming , some ask why we don't just follow Singapore and Hong Kong and import everything. Singapore's protein self-sufficiency rate was affected by pandemic import/export disruptions, so they plan to raise it to 30%by 2030. But people are asking about milk, not general protein—what does importing all our milk have to do with protein rates? If there's suddenly no milk, we can use other proteins. The point is, milk isn't suitable for local production, so why not import everything like Singapore? Does a high protein rate require us to.

force domestic milk production? And like this comment says, "Just in case, Taiwan would still have milk to drink." But as the founder of a local dairy brand and industry insiders have pointed out, all the feed for Taiwan's dairy cows is imported! If the worst were to happen, you’d be out of feed too. Is Taiwan’s high self-sufficiency rate for milk even real? Isn't it just keeping import shares low through protectionist quotas ? Is this just to maintain the sky-high prices of domestic milk? If we're talking about protein self-sufficiency and nutrition, the Health Promotion Administration states that Taiwanese people consume insufficient dairy—only half of what people in the West do, or even less. So, is Taiwan raising self-sufficiency for the sake of public. health? Not at all. With the current supply shortage, do you know what the Taiwanese dairy industry is doing? They’re cutting production and planning to cull dairy cows. When people don't even have enough milk to drink, they’re cutting supply. Does that look like an attempt to boost self-sufficiency? Self-sufficiency is a fake issue; we import all our feed. If there were a naval blockade, where would that self-sufficiency be? I want to ask: if you think dairy is a staple like rice or wheat, shouldn't the government regulate its price? Shouldn't they be ensuring the supply volume? Then why let Taiwanese milk become the most expensive in the world, or even create trade. barriers through legislation? They even use programs like "Classroom Milk" to treat students like recycling bins, making them drink it to clear out inventory. If dairy is truly an essential good, we should ensure supply instead of cutting production when per capita intake is already low. We should make prices reasonable and bring down those sky-high costs, rather than playing games to maintain them. If you claim to believe in market mechanisms, don't push farmers out whenever New Zealand is mentioned. You can't demand market mechanisms when selling for a high price, then beg for protection when it's time to compete. Didn't you say you. wanted market mechanisms? If we're talking market mechanisms, let the inefficient fail. How can you claim there's a market mechanism with so many protectionist measures? Wheat is a vital food source and we import that freely without worrying about a blockade cutting off our noodles. So why protect dairy—which is practically a luxury item in Taiwan—and hide behind farmers? Stop using "local" and "fresh" as an excuse to play the victim. After electronic watches arrived, they outperformed mechanical watches in value, so mechanical watches pivoted to luxury. When ballpoint pens arrived, they outperformed fountain pens, so fountain pens went luxury. If domestic milk can't compete in commercial scale or if its. technology is behind global standards, it should definitely pivot toward premium or high-quality development, just like mechanical watches. But you've stated that this is a staple commodity and a daily necessity. I don't oppose local milk brands focusing on their specialty, but they should just remain niche specialty brands. If a premium milk brand thinks those with deep pockets should buy them, it's like the wheat in Daya, Taichung. Surely not everyone needs to produce luxury boutique products, right? You can't make all cars unaffordable for the average person; there must be cheaper options available as well. Taiwanese milk should take a backseat and stay niche, like supercars; whoever wants to splurge can buy them, but the mass market should be. dominated by imported milk. This means Taiwan could import millions of tons of milk from the US and New Zealand annually, but right now, locally produced milk accounts for 90%, and they’re all obsessed with emphasizing their "specialty." Is it really necessary to block all Taiwanese people from the opportunity to buy milk at a reasonable price just for this? If every brand ends up doing this, then can we still really call milk a necessity? Thankfully, wheat is almost entirely imported; otherwise, all your flour-based foods would cost three or four times more right now. y.

=============

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUqJ2OBfB6s

百靈果《The KK Show 387》邀請鮮乳坊創辦人阿嘉，討論為什麼台灣牛奶比日本貴，以及台灣乳業與進口牛奶的差異。

但訪談中提到的體細胞數（SCC）、美國乳源標準、牛隻生長激素（rbST）、牛奶殺菌方式、營養與保存期限，真的足以證明台灣牛奶比進口牛奶更好嗎？

這支影片針對該集訪談內容進行資料查核與評論，補上幾個容易被忽略的關鍵問題：

本片討論重點

體細胞數（SCC）：台灣30萬、美國75萬，法規上限比較寬鬆，就代表實際乳源品質比較差嗎？

美國與紐西蘭的實際體細胞數據，和台灣公開的乳源數據相比，究竟如何？

美國法律允許使用rbST，是否代表美國乳牛普遍都在使用？

歐盟、紐西蘭對rbST的規範又是什麼？

台灣鮮乳的實際殺菌方式，和進口乳的高溫處理有什麼差異？

牛奶營養、風味與保存期限的比較，是否交代了完整的背景？

法規容許的上限，不等於市場實際的平均表現。法律允許使用，也不代表市場普遍使用。

我沒有要替進口牛奶背書，也不是要替國產牛奶護航。消費者應該得到完整的資訊，而不是只看到對某一方有利的比較。

item.content:encoded:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUqJ2OBfB6s

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開台灣國產鮮乳與進口鮮乳保存期限巨大差異背後的真正原因。
  • 釐清大眾及主流媒體長年誤將台灣鮮乳視為「低溫殺菌」的認知盲區與事實真相。
  • 深入分析業界代表在訪談中「只說一半實話」如何無形中誤導消費者對風味與品質的判斷。

摘要

百靈果專訪鮮乳坊引發的保存期爭議

作者指出，知名Podcast節目《百靈果》在專訪鮮乳坊創辦人時，主持人凱莉提出了一個民眾普遍好奇的核心疑問：為何台灣鮮乳的保存期限通常只有約十三天，而進口鮮乳卻能保存三十天甚至八、九十天？面對該提問，受訪者僅表示國外也有短效期的鮮乳、不同殺菌方式會影響保存期限與口感，並提及梅納反應對風味的影響，卻始終未正面解釋關鍵的差異本質，令許多期待聽到真相的觀眾感到受訪者在刻意迴避。

台灣鮮乳普遍採用超高溫殺菌的真相

作者進一步強調，一般民眾容易誤以為台灣鮮乳之所以保存期限短，是因為採用了歐美常見的72度低溫巴氏殺菌；但事實上，農業數據與消基會資料均證實，台灣高達99%的鮮乳都是採用125度至138度的超高溫滅菌（UHT）技術。國產鮮乳與進口乳在殺菌溫度上並無顯著較低，甚至殺菌溫度可能更高，然而台灣鮮乳卻只能冷藏保存不到兩週。作者質疑，這其中的關鍵其實是無菌充填技術與保存條件，受訪者卻將問題歸咎於殺菌溫度差異，完全偏離了核心事實。

只說一半的實話對消費者認知的誤導

作者認為，在訪談中「只說一半的實話」比說錯話更為嚴重，因為缺少關鍵資訊會導致觀眾自行腦補錯誤結論，甚至連主流媒體記者都長年誤報台灣鮮乳是低溫殺菌。此外，受訪者稱進口乳因高溫產生梅納反應而風味不如鮮乳純淨，但事實上台灣各大品牌同樣採用超高溫殺菌，若依此邏輯也會產生梅納反應。作者呼籲乳品產業應公開透明地呈現完整科學事實，而非利用資訊落差與避重就輕的話術誤導消費者對國產鮮乳與進口乳的認知。

================================================

The Bailingguo podcast invited the founder of Milk Man; this interview is incredibly packed with insights. For instance, Kylie asked, "Why does Taiwanese fresh milk expire so quickly? ""Foreign milk can last for 30 days." Anyone who knows the truth about Taiwan’s fresh milk must think that was a great question, right? So satisfying! Asking him directly to his face to see how he’d answer—yeah, why is that? The comments section also felt it hit the nail on the head, but naturally, he didn't really answer it; he just dodged the question. For those of you who know the truth, let's not spoil it yet. For viewers watching on a computer, I suggest opening the original interview video as well and checking each segment along the timeline; if the original. makes you want to roll your eyes, you can come back here to see how he actually responded. He said that abroad there is also shorter-shelf-life milk, that everyone uses different sterilization methods, and with Taiwan's current methods, it's about two weeks and must be refrigerated; there’s a difference in flavor and texture, and some people don't like the Maillard reaction taste, so [his] fresh milk is purer. It looks like he answered it, right? Different shelf lives because domestic and foreign sterilization methods differ, but that’s not what the audience wants to know. "Everyone uses different sterilization methods"—who is "everyone"? When you say "different," who exactly is being compared to whom? You replied that there is also short-shelf-life milk abroad, usually at 72 to 75 degrees for 15 seconds, sold locally for quick consumption; that statement itself isn't wrong, but what Kylie was asking about was the imported milk we see in Taiwan—why is its shelf life longer? Now, can I be the one to ask? Hitting the nail on the head isn't enough; we need to cut to the bone and ask who is being compared to whom: when Taiwan's Kuang Chuan, Uni-President, Richi, Lin Fengying, or even your Milk Man, are compared to American imports like Costco’s Kirkland or Foremost, why can theirs last 85 or 90 days while. Taiwan's only lasts 13? "Different sterilization methods"—how, exactly, are they different? When viewers see that Taiwan's fresh milk only lasts 13 days, might they think it's the same 72- degree low-temperature pasteurization used locally in Europe and America? How innocent, how kind—so it's different from the ultra-high temperature used for imported milk? The truth is, Taiwan's fresh milk is all ultra-high temperature ! Isn't the agricultural data right here ? 99%is UHT; the Consumers 'Foundation also says Taiwanese milk is basically long-life milk, 125 to 135 degrees, while imported milk is 135 or 138 degrees—how many degrees lower is that,. really? So is*this*what you meant by " different"? Let's look at the dairy industry: 138 degrees for 1.5 to 2 seconds, yet it only lasts 13 days refrigerated. Australian UHT milk is 135 degrees for 1 to 2 seconds and can be stored at room temperature for 12 months . Yes, the sterilization methods are different. Domestic milk is three degrees higher than imported milk. It's different, but because it's at a higher temperature, the shelf life is actually shorter? Is that how it works? Or is it because there's no aseptic filling? Although some comments felt it was spot on, others felt the guest was shifting the focus and dodging questions, only saying what they wanted to say. 百靈果《The KK Show 387》邀請鮮乳坊創辦人阿嘉，討論為什麼台灣牛奶比日本貴，以及台灣乳業與進口牛奶的差異。

但訪談中提到的體細胞數（SCC）、美國乳源標準、牛隻生長激素（rbST）、牛奶殺菌方式、營養與保存期限，真的足以證明台灣牛奶比進口牛奶更好嗎？

這支影片針對該集訪談內容進行資料查核與評論，補上幾個容易被忽略的關鍵問題：

本片討論重點

體細胞數（SCC）：台灣30萬、美國75萬，法規上限比較寬鬆，就代表實際乳源品質比較差嗎？

美國與紐西蘭的實際體細胞數據，和台灣公開的乳源數據相比，究竟如何？

美國法律允許使用rbST，是否代表美國乳牛普遍都在使用？

歐盟、紐西蘭對rbST的規範又是什麼？

台灣鮮乳的實際殺菌方式，和進口乳的高溫處理有什麼差異？

牛奶營養、風味與保存期限的比較，是否交代了完整的背景？

法規容許的上限，不等於市場實際的平均表現。法律允許使用，也不代表市場普遍使用。

我沒有要替進口牛奶背書，也不是要替國產牛奶護航。消費者應該得到完整的資訊，而不是只看到對某一方有利的比較。
